'''Wolverhampton Wanderers Football Club''' ({{IPAc-en|audio=en-uk-Wolverhampton.ogg|ˌ|w|ʊ|l|v|ər|ˈ|h|æ|m|p|t|ən}} {{respell|WUUL|vər|HAMP|tən}}), commonly referred to as '''Wolves''',<ref name="nickname" /> is a professional [[association football|football]] club based in [[Wolverhampton]], England. The club competes in the [[EFL Championship]], the second tier of [[English football league system|English football]]. The club has played at [[Molineux Stadium]] since moving from [[Dudley Road]] in 1889. The club's traditional kit consists of [[old gold]] shirts and socks with black shorts. Since 1979, the kit has also featured the club's "wolf's head" logo. Long-standing rivalries exist with other clubs from the [[West Midlands (county)|West Midlands]], including [[Aston Villa F.C.|Aston Villa]], [[Stoke City F.C.|Stoke City]], and [[Birmingham City F.C.|Birmingham City]] but the main one being the [[Black Country derby]] contested with [[West Bromwich Albion F.C.|West Bromwich Albion]]. Since 2016, the club has been owned by the Chinese conglomerate [[Fosun International]].

Formed as '''St. Luke's F.C.''' in 1877, the club changed name to Wolverhampton Wanderers two years later and became one of the founding members of the [[English Football League|Football League]] in [[1888–89 Football League|1888]]. They won the [[FA Cup]] for the first time in [[1893 FA Cup Final|1893]], and again as a [[Football League Second Division|Second Division]] team in [[1908 FA Cup Final|1908]] following the club's relegation two years previously. They fell to the third tier in 1923, but went on to win the [[Football League Third Division North|Third Division North]] in 1923–24 and the Second Division in [[1931–32 Football League|1931–32]]. The team was crowned [[List of English football champions|English League champions]] three times – in [[1953–54 Football League|1953–54]], [[1957–58 Football League|1957–58]] and [[1958–59 Football League|1958–59]] – all under the management of [[Stan Cullis]]. Wolves also won another two FA Cup finals, in [[1949 FA Cup Final|1949]] and [[1960 FA Cup Final|1960]]. Relegated in 1965, after 26 consecutive seasons in the top flight, they secured promotion back to the First Division in [[1966–67 Football League|1966–67]]. Wolves won the [[EFL Cup|League Cup]] in [[1974 Football League Cup Final|1974]] and [[1980 Football League Cup Final|1980]], and again won the Second Division title in [[1976–77 Football League|1976–77]].

Wolves suffered a financial crisis during the [[Early 1980s recession|early-1980s recession]] that led to the club coming close to [[liquidation]] in 1982. In the five seasons between [[1981-82 Football League|1981–82]] and [[1985-86 Football League|1985–86]] Wolves were relegated four times (although there was also one promotion in [[1982–83 Football League|1982–83]]), meaning the club ended up in what was then the [[Football League Fourth Division]] (now [[EFL League Two]]) for the first (and so far only) time in the club's history. However, the club immediately started a swift turn-around, and having been beaten in the inaugural Football League play-off final in [[1987 Football League Fourth Division play-off Final|1987]], Wolves won the [[Football League Fourth Division|Fourth Division]] and [[EFL Trophy|Football League Trophy]] titles in [[1987–88 Football League|1987–88]], followed by the [[Football League Third Division|Third Division]] title in [[1988-89 Football League Third Division|1988–89]].

After fourteen seasons in the second tier between 1989 and 2003, Wolves reached the [[Premier League]], founded in 1992, for the first time with victory in the [[2003 Football League First Division play-off Final|2003 play-offs]], though they were relegated after a single season in the top division on this occasion. Wolves won the [[EFL Championship|Championship]] in 2008–09 to return to the Premier League, but endured relegation in [[2011-12 Premier League|2011–12]], followed by relegation again (to [[EFL League One]]) in [[2012-13 Football League Championship|2012–13]]. The club then returned to the Premier League after first winning the [[EFL League One|League One]] title in 2013–14, followed by another Championship title in 2017–18.

After becoming one of the first British clubs to install [[floodlight]]s at its home ground in 1953, Wolves arranged televised "floodlit friendlies" against leading overseas club sides between 1953 and 1956, the most notable being the famous Honved game, which were instrumental in the launch of the [[UEFA Champions League|European Cup]] (now known as the UEFA Champions League) in [[1955–56 European Cup|1955]]. Wolves reached the quarter-finals of the competition in [[1959–60 European Cup|1959–60]] as well as the semi-finals of the [[1960–61 European Cup Winners' Cup]] and the [[1972 UEFA Cup Final|inaugural UEFA Cup Final]] in 1972. Following a 39-year absence from UEFA competitions, they reached the [[2019–20 UEFA Europa League knockout phase#Matches 3|UEFA Europa League finals in 2020]].

===Formation and the Football League (1879–1893)===
In the 2000 edition of ''The Rough Guide to English Football'', the history section on the Wolves page begins: "The very name Wolves thunders from the pages of English football history".<ref name="Rough">Goldstein, Dan (editor). The Rough Guide to English Football (2000), page 582. Rough Guides Ltd.</ref> As with several other clubs, [[Everton F.C.|Everton]] for example, Wolves had humble beginnings shaped by the twin influences of [[cricket]] and the [[Christian Church|church]]. The club was founded in 1877 as ''' St. Luke's F.C.''' by John Baynton and [[John Brodie (footballer born 1862)|John Brodie]], two pupils of St Luke's Church School in [[Blakenhall]], who had been presented with a football by their headmaster Harry Barcroft.<ref name="Matthews">{{cite book |author=Matthews, Tony |title=Wolverhampton Wanderers: The Complete Record |year=2008 |publisher=Breedon Books |location=Derby |isbn=978-1-85983-632-3}}</ref> The team played its first game on 13 January 1877 against a reserve side from [[Stafford Road F.C.|Stafford Road]], later merging with the football section of a local cricket club called Blakenhall Wanderers to form '''Wolverhampton Wanderers''' in August 1879.<ref name="Rough"/><ref name="Matthews"/> Having initially played on two strips of land in the town, they relocated to a more substantial venue on [[Dudley Road]] in 1881, before lifting their first trophy in 1884 when they won the Wrekin Cup, during a season in which they played their first [[FA Cup]] tie.<ref name="Matthews"/> Having become professional, the club were nominated to become one of the twelve founder members of the [[Football League]] in 1888,<ref>{{cite web |title=The Father of The Football League |publisher=[[The Football League]] |url=http://www.football-league.co.uk/footballleaguenews/20130227/the-father-of-the-football-league_2293334_3091039 |date=27 February 2013 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130302121558/http://www.football-league.co.uk/footballleaguenews/20130227/the-father-of-the-football-league_2293334_3091039 |archive-date=2 March 2013 }}</ref> in which they played in the first round of Football League fixtures ever staged, against [[Aston Villa F.C.|Aston Villa]] on 8 September 1888.<ref name="FL History">{{cite web |url=http://www.football-league.co.uk/page/History/HistoryDetail/0,,10794~1357277,00.html |title=History of the Football League |publisher=[[The Football League]] |date=22 September 2010 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110501121005/http://www.football-league.co.uk/page/History/HistoryDetail/0%2C%2C10794~1357277%2C00.html |archive-date=1 May 2011 }}</ref> They ended the inaugural season in third place, as well as reaching their [[1889 FA Cup Final|first FA Cup Final]], losing 0–3 to the first [[Double (association football)#England|"Double"]] winners, [[Preston North End F.C.|Preston North End]]. At the conclusion of the campaign the club relocated for a final time when they moved to [[Molineux Stadium|Molineux]], then a pleasure park known as the Molineux Grounds.<ref name="Matthews"/>

===FA Cup success and world war years (1893–1950)===
[[File:Wolverhampton wanderers 1893.jpg|thumb|Wolves' 1893 FA Cup-winning team]]

Wolves lifted the FA Cup for the first time in [[1893 FA Cup Final|1893]] when they beat [[Everton F.C.|Everton]] 1–0, and made a third [[1896 FA Cup Final|FA Cup Final appearance in 1896]]. The club added a second FA Cup Final triumph (a 3–1 win against [[Newcastle United]]) to their 1893 success in [[1908 FA Cup Final|1908]], two years after having dropped into the [[Football League Second Division|Second Division]] for the first time. After struggling during the years either side of the First World War to regain their place in the top division (a period that was punctuated by another [[1921 FA Cup Final|FA Cup Final appearance in 1921]]), the club suffered a [[1922–23 Football League#Second Division|further relegation in 1923]], entering the [[Football League Third Division North|Third Division (North)]], which they [[1923–24 Football League Third Division North|won at the first attempt]]. Eight years after returning to the Second Division, Wolves regained their top-flight status as [[1931-32 Football League Second Division|Second Division Champions]] under [[Frank Buckley (footballer)|Major Frank Buckley]] after twenty-six years away. With Buckley at the helm the team became established as one of the leading club sides in England in the years leading up to the Second World War, as they finished runners-up in the league twice in succession ([[1937–38 Football League#First Division|1937–38]] & [[1938–39 Football League#First Division|1938–39]]), as well as reaching the [[1939 FA Cup Final|last pre-war FA Cup Final]], in which they suffered a shock defeat to [[Portsmouth F.C.|Portsmouth]].<ref>{{cite news |title=The Cup Final: Today's prospects at Wembley| newspaper=The Times |location=London |date=29 April 1939|page=4}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://espnfc.com/columns/story?id=786336&sec=englandopinion&root=englandopinion&cc=5739#|title=FA Cup final upsets|date=14 May 2010|publisher=[[ESPN]]|access-date=3 April 2013|archive-date=3 January 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140103021630/http://espnfc.com/columns/story?id=786336&sec=englandopinion&root=englandopinion&cc=5739|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/sport/football/teams/stoke-city/8509939/FA-Cup-Final-2011-Seven-Wembley-upsets-to-give-Stoke-City-hope-as-they-start-underdogs-against-Manchester-City.html |archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/archive/20220110/https://www.telegraph.co.uk/sport/football/teams/stoke-city/8509939/FA-Cup-Final-2011-Seven-Wembley-upsets-to-give-Stoke-City-hope-as-they-start-underdogs-against-Manchester-City.html |archive-date=10 January 2022 |url-access=subscription |url-status=live |title=Seven Wembley upsets to give Stoke City hope as they start underdogs against Manchester City |date=12 May 2011|work=[[The Daily Telegraph]]}}{{cbignore}}</ref> In [[1937–38 Football League#First Division|1937–38]] Wolves came within a whisker of winning the club's first English league title: a win in the side's last game away to [[Sunderland F.C.|Sunderland]] would have clinched things, but in the event Wolves lost 0–1 and thus ended the campaign one point behind the eventual champions, [[Arsenal F.C.|Arsenal]].<ref>Matthews, Tony (1994). ''Wolves, The Complete Record'', page 31. Breedon Books Publishing Company. {{ISBN|1859830005}}.</ref> One of the things Major Buckley and his Wolves side attracted a lot of attention for in the last two full seasons prior to the suspension of league football during the Second World War was Buckley's insistence that his players be injected with monkey gland extract to enhance their stamina and performance, a practice that the Football League disapproved of but did not prohibit.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.theblizzard.co.uk/article/monkey-glands|title=Monkey Glands – Major Frank Buckley took Wolves to 1930s prominence with dubious injections|date=1 December 2017|publisher=www.theblizzard.co.uk|access-date=6 December 2017|archive-date=6 November 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201106200914/https://www.theblizzard.co.uk/article/monkey-glands|url-status=dead}}</ref>

When league football resumed after the Second World War, Wolves suffered yet another final day failure in the First Division. Just as in 1938, victory in their last match would have won the title but a 2–1 loss to title rivals [[Liverpool F.C.|Liverpool]] meant that Liverpool were crowned champions instead.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.lfchistory.net/Articles/Article/2464|title=Billy wins his only League title in 1947|publisher=LFChistory.net|access-date=3 April 2013|archive-date=9 October 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121009102804/http://www.lfchistory.net/Articles/Article/2464|url-status=live}}</ref> This game had been the last in a Wolves shirt for [[Stan Cullis]], and a year later he became manager of the club. In Cullis's first season in charge, he led Wolves to a first major honour in 41 years as they beat [[Leicester City F.C.|Leicester City]] to lift the [[1949 FA Cup Final|FA Cup]], and a year later, [[1949–50 Football League#First Division|only goal average prevented Wolves winning the league title]].<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.theguardian.com/news/2001/mar/01/guardianobituaries.football |title=Stan Cullis |first=Brian |last=Glanville |work=The Guardian |date=1 March 2001 |access-date=15 October 2020 |archive-date=15 December 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181215125948/https://www.theguardian.com/news/2001/mar/01/guardianobituaries.football |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.rsssf.org/engpaul/FLA/1949-50.html |title=Season 1949–50 |website=RSSSF |access-date=15 October 2020 |archive-date=27 July 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220727201340/https://www.rsssf.org/engpaul/FLA/1949-50.html |url-status=live }}</ref>

===The Stan Cullis era (1950–1960)===
[[File:Wolverhampton Wanderers F.C. 1955.jpg|thumb|305px|Wolverhampton Wanderers F.C., side at 1955 with following players, from left standing: [[Bill Slater (footballer)|Bill Slater]], [[Bill Shorthouse]], [[Bert Williams (footballer, born 1920)|Bert Williams]], [[Ron Flowers]], [[Eddie Stuart]]; front row: [[Johnny Hancocks]], [[Peter Broadbent (footballer)|Peter Broadbent]], [[Roy Swinbourne]], [[Billy Wright (footballer, born 1924)|Billy Wright]] ([[Captain (sports)|captain]]), [[Dennis Wilshaw]] and [[Jimmy Mullen (footballer, born 1923)|Jimmy Mullen]].]]
The 1950s were by far the most successful period in the club's history.<ref name="Cullis">{{cite news |url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/sport2/hi/football/1193951.stm |title=Wolves legend Cullis dies |publisher=BBC Sport |date=28 February 2001 |access-date=27 March 2013 |archive-date=6 April 2003 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20030406083829/http://news.bbc.co.uk/sport1/hi/football/1193951.stm |url-status=live }}</ref> Captained by [[Billy Wright (footballer, born 1924)|Billy Wright]], Wolves finally claimed the league championship for the first time in [[1953–54 Football League#First Division|1953–54]], overhauling [[Black Country derby|local rivals]] [[West Bromwich Albion F.C.|West Bromwich Albion]] late in the season. Two further titles were soon won in successive years ([[1957–58 Football League#First Division|1957–58]] and [[1958–59 Football League#First Division|1958–59]]), as Wolves vied with [[Manchester United]] to be acknowledged the premier team in English football at that juncture. Wolves were renowned both for the club's domestic success and for the staging of high-profile "floodlit friendlies" against other top club sides from around the world.<ref name="European">{{cite book |author=Shipley, John |title=Wolves Against the World |year=2003 |publisher=The History Press |location=Stroud |isbn=0-7524-2947-7}}</ref> Wolves had become one of the first club sides in Britain to invest in floodlighting in 1953 at a cost of £10,000<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.birminghammail.co.uk/sport/football/football-news/wolves-61-years-ago-today-8280713 |title=When Wolverhampton Wanderers invented European football |work=[[Birmingham Mail]] |date=13 December 2017 |access-date=20 March 2018 |archive-date=20 March 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180320105539/https://www.birminghammail.co.uk/sport/football/football-news/wolves-61-years-ago-today-8280713 |url-status=live }}</ref> ({{inflation|UK|10000|1953|fmt=eq|cursign=£|r=-5}}). Perhaps [[Wolverhampton Wanderers F.C. v Budapest Honvéd FC|the most famed of these friendlies]] saw Wolves defeat a [[Budapest Honvéd FC|Honvéd]] side including many members of the [[Hungary national football team|Hungarian national team]] that had recently humbled [[England national football team|England]] twice, leading the national media to proclaim Wolves "Champions of the World".<ref name="UEFA">{{cite web |url=http://www.uefa.com/news/newsid=419682.html |title=Hats off to Hanot |date=12 May 2006 |publisher=[[UEFA]] |access-date=26 March 2013 |archive-date=12 April 2013 |archive-url=https://archive.today/20130412015611/http://www.uefa.com/news/newsid=419682.html |url-status=dead }}</ref> This became the final spur for [[Gabriel Hanot]], the editor of ''[[L'Équipe]]'', to propose [[European Cup and UEFA Champions League history|the creation of the European Cup]] (later rebranded as the [[UEFA Champions League]]). Wolves were one of the first British clubs to participate.<ref name="UEFA"/> In the 1957–58 season, Wolves defeated [[Real Madrid]] 5–4 (3–2 in Wolverhampton and 2–2 in Madrid) in home and away friendlies.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://origin.expressandstar.mna.arcpublishing.com/sport/football/wolverhampton-wanderers-fc/2016/02/16/classic-match-report-wolves-3-real-madrid-2-1957-2/ |title=Classic match report – Wolves 3 Real Madrid 2, 1957 |publisher=Express and Star |date=16 February 2016 |access-date=18 May 2018 |archive-date=19 May 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180519032625/https://origin.expressandstar.mna.arcpublishing.com/sport/football/wolverhampton-wanderers-fc/2016/02/16/classic-match-report-wolves-3-real-madrid-2-1957-2/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

===Cup success in the '60s and '70s (1960–1980)===
[[File:Wolverhampton Wanderers FC League Performance.svg|thumb|Chart of yearly performance of Wolves in the [[English football league system|English Football League system]].]]

The 1960s began with [[1960 FA Cup Final|a fourth FA Cup victory]] and Wolves almost achieved the [[Double (association football)|first League and FA Cup 'double' of the 20th century]] in English football. They were pipped to the league title by a point on the final day of the season by [[Burnley F.C.|Burnley]]. Despite that bright start to the decade, the 1960s saw Wolves begin to decline. After finishing as [[1959-60 Football League#First Division|league runners-up in 1959–60]] and a creditable third-place league finish in [[Tottenham Hotspur]]'s [[1960-61 Football League#First Division|'double'-winning season]], the team faded and Cullis himself was dismissed after sixteen years in post in September 1964 after a disastrous start to the [[1964-65 Football League First Division|1964–65 season]].<ref name="Cullis"/> Cullis's dismissal did not prevent the season ending with relegation (the first time Wolves had known relegation since [[1922–23 Football League#Second Division|1922–23]]) and the club's first spell outside the top division since 1932. Exile from the top flight lasted only two seasons however, as Wolves were [[1966–67 Football League#Second Division|promoted in 1967]] as Second Division runners-up.<ref name="Positions">{{cite web |url=https://www.footballhistory.org/club/wolverhampton-wanderers.html |title=Wolverhampton Wanderers FC - short history and facts |website=footballhistory.org |access-date=18 October 2020 |archive-date=18 October 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201018020405/https://www.footballhistory.org/club/wolverhampton-wanderers.html |url-status=live }}</ref>

During the close season in 1967, Wolves played a mini-season in North America as part of the fledgling [[United Soccer Association|United Soccer Association league]] which imported clubs from Europe and South America. Playing as the "[[Los Angeles Wolves]]", they won the Western Division and ultimately the championship by defeating the Eastern Division champions [[Washington Whips]] (import of [[Aberdeen F.C.|Aberdeen]]) in a final decider.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.wolvesheroes.com/2009/05/04/usa-1967/|title=USA, 1967: Life in the Fast Lane|date=4 May 2009|publisher=Wolves Heroes|access-date=3 April 2013|archive-date=24 December 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131224101315/http://www.wolvesheroes.com/2009/05/04/usa-1967/|url-status=live}}</ref>

The club's return to the English top flight in 1967 heralded another period of relative success under [[Bill McGarry]], with [[1970–71 Football League#First Division|a fourth place league finish in 1971]] qualifying Wolves for the newly created [[UEFA Europa League|UEFA Cup]].<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.rsssf.org/engpaul/FLA/1970-71.html |title=England 1970/71 |website=RSSSF |access-date=18 Final|the UEFA Cup final]], they defeated [[Juventus FC|Juventus]] and [[Ferencvárosi TC|Ferencváros]] before losing to [[Tottenham Hotspur F.C.|Tottenham Hotspur]] 3–2 on aggregate; a 2–1 home defeat ===Financial crisis, decline and recovery (1980–1990)===
The multi-million pound rebuilding of the Molineux Street Stand in 1979 was the catalyst for the club's near-financial ruin during the next decade. Plunging match attendances in the early 1980s,<ref>{{cite book |title=Wolves: The Complete Record|first=Tony|last=Matthews |isbn=1-85983-000-5|year=1994|publisher=Breedon Books Publishing Company|page=73}}</ref> at least partly due to [[Early 1980s recession#United Kingdom|recession in both the national and local economies]], and consequent difficulties in repaying the loans taken out to fund the new John Ireland Stand, led the club to [[receivership]] and relegation in 1982. After a shareholders’ rebellion against Harry Marshall led by Wolverhampton insurance-broker Roger Jeffrey Hipkiss,<ref name="OG 2022 ">{{cite web|url=https://www.wolves.co.uk/news/features/20220802-old-gold-40-years-on-from-when-wolves-first-faced-extinction/|title=40 years on from when Wolves First Faced Extinction|publisher=Wolverhampton Wanderers F. C. Official Website|access-date=1 September 2022}}</ref><ref name="WH RJH ">{{cite web|url=https://www.wolvesheroes.com/remembering-roger/|title=Remembering Roger|publisher=Wolverhampton Wanderers F. C. Official Website|access-date=1 September 2022}}</ref><ref name="AW ">{{cite web|url=https://alwayswolves.co.uk/doug-hope-the-bhattis-bank-loans-and-bust/|title=Doug Hope - The Bhatti's, Bank Loans And Bust|publisher=Always Wolves Website|access-date=1 March 2024}}</ref> the club was saved from liquidation at the last minute when it was purchased by a consortium fronted by Hipkiss's close friend<ref name="WH RJH "/> and its former player [[Derek Dougan]].<ref name="1982 deal">{{cite news |title=Wolves are saved by last-minute deal| newspaper=The Times |location=London |date=31 July 1982|page=17}}</ref> The takeover, financed by two Saudi brothers, Mahmud and Mohammad Bhatti of the company Allied Properties,<ref>{{cite news |title=Wolves 'will have to pay own way'| newspaper=The Times |location=London |date=9 August 1982|page=15}}</ref> brought immediate [[1982–83 Football League Second Division|promotion back to the First Division]] under manager [[Graham Hawkins]], but the Bhattis' failure to invest sufficiently in the club soon saw things unravel, and the team suffered three consecutive relegations through the football divisions under different managers,<ref name="Crisis3">{{cite news|title=Wolves: What's gone wrong at Molineux?|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/football/21589401|publisher=BBC Sport|date=1 March 2013|access-date=13 February 2018|archive-date=17 October 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131017153618/http://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/0/football/21589401|url-status=live}}</ref> as well as the almost-constant threat of the club being wound-up.<ref name="Crisis1">{{cite news |title=Wolves in new crisis| newspaper=The Times |location=London |date=6 December 1982|page=23}}</ref><ref name="Crisis2">{{cite news |title=Wolves try to suspend winding-up order| newspaper=The Times |location=London |date=30 July 1985|page=25}}</ref>

In 1986, with the club again in receivership, a deal saw [[Wolverhampton City Council]] purchase the stadium and surrounding land, while a local developer paid off the club's outstanding debts in return for planning permission to develop the land adjacent to the stadium.<ref name="1986 deal">{{cite news |title=Wolves in the clear| newspaper=The Times |location=London |date=6 August 1986|page=32}}</ref> The 1986–87 season saw Wolves' first campaign in the Fourth Division where, with the guidance of new manager [[Graham Turner]], and goals from [[Steve Bull]], who ultimately scored a club record 306 goals,<ref>{{cite news |url=http://www.wolves.co.uk/news/article/hof-steve-bull-2009-421293.aspx?pageView=full |title=Steve Bull |date=16 January 2009 |publisher=Wolverhampton Wanderers F.C |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304054807/http://www.wolves.co.uk/news/article/hof-steve-bull-2009-421293.aspx?pageView=full |archive-date=4 March 2016 }}</ref> the team reached [[1987 Football League Fourth Division play-off Final|the final of the inaugural play-offs]] but were denied promotion by [[Aldershot F.C.|Aldershot]]. Building on that, in the next two seasons the team achieved both the [[1987–88 Football League Fourth Division|Fourth]] and [[1988–89 Football League#Third Division|Third Division]] championships, and won the [[1988 Football League Trophy Final]] at [[Wembley Stadium (1923)|Wembley]].

===The Hayward years (1990–2007)===
[[File:Wolves Football League Championship 2008–09 030509.jpg|left|thumb|Celebrating the Championship title in 2009]]

Lifelong fan [[Jack Hayward]] purchased the club in 1990 and immediately funded the extensive redevelopment of a by then dilapidated Molineux into a modern all-seater stadium.<ref name="1990 deal">{{cite news |title=Hayward pledge to restore the greatness of Wolves| newspaper=The Times |location=London |date=11 May 1990|page=43}}</ref> With work completed in 1993, Hayward redirected his investment onto the playing side in an attempt to win promotion to the newly formed [[Premier League]]. Despite substantial spending, neither [[Graham Taylor (footballer)|Graham Taylor]] nor [[Mark McGhee]] could fulfil this, both managers leading the team to play-off defeats at the semi-final stages in [[1995 Football League play-offs#First Division|1995]] and [[1997 Football League play-offs#First Division|1997]] respectively. It was not until 2003 that Wolves were promoted, when they defeated [[Sheffield United F.C.|Sheffield United]] 3–0 in [[2003 Football League First Division play-off Final|the play-off final]] under [[Dave Jones (footballer, born 1956)|Dave Jones]] to end a 19-year absence from the top level.<ref name="2003 promotion">{{cite news |url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/sport2/hi/football/teams/w/wolverhampton_wanderers/2938952.stm |title=Hayward's dream come true |date=27 May 2003 |publisher=[[BBC Sport]] |access-date=27 March 2013 |archive-date=19 April 2004 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20040419040844/http://news.bbc.co.uk/sport1/hi/football/teams/w/wolverhampton_wanderers/2938952.stm |url-status=live }}</ref> Their stay proved short-lived however as they were immediately relegated back to the newly retitled [[EFL Championship]].

The club's traditional colours of gold and black allude to [[Wolverhampton City Council|the city council]]'s motto "'''out of darkness cometh light'''" with the two colours representing light and darkness respectively.<ref>{{cite news|title=1984: Wolves' recurring nightmare|url=https://www.theguardian.com/football/2003/may/25/sport.comment2|work=The Guardian|date=25 May 2003|access-date=13 December 2016|archive-date=1 December 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161201175133/https://www.theguardian.com/football/2003/may/25/sport.comment2|url-status=live}}</ref> Although the team's original colours upon formation were red and white, adopted from the school colours of St Lukes, for much of their history their home colours have been their distinctive old gold shirts with black shorts.<ref>{{cite news |title=Wolverhampton Wanderers |url=http://thebeautifulhistory.wordpress.com/clubs/wolverhampton-wanderers/ |publisher=The Beautiful History |access-date=14 February 2013 |archive-date=14 December 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121214094303/http://thebeautifulhistory.wordpress.com/clubs/wolverhampton-wanderers/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

In the early decades of the club a variety of shirt designs using these colours were created, including stripes and diagonal halves, until the continual usage of a plain shirt design since the 1930s.<ref name="HistoricalKits">{{cite news |title=Wolverhampton Wanderers – Historical Kits |url=http://www.historicalkits.co.uk/Wolverhampton_Wanderers/Wolverhampton_Wanderers.htm |publisher=Historicalkits.co.uk |access-date=25 February 2009 |archive-date=16 February 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090216184942/http://historicalkits.co.uk/Wolverhampton_Wanderers/Wolverhampton_Wanderers.htm |url-status=live }}</ref> Before the 1960s a darker shade of gold was used,<ref>The "old gold" colour was briefly revived during 2000–02.</ref> known as "[[old gold]]", which is still often cited in the media as the club's colour.<ref>{{cite news |title=Old gold turns to dross for Wolves |url=https://www.theguardian.com/football/blog/2012/apr/19/wolves-terry-connor-relegation |work=The Guardian |date=19 April 2012 |access-date=13 December 2016 |archive-date=9 November 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161109221444/https://www.theguardian.com/football/blog/2012/apr/19/wolves-terry-connor-relegation |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=Old Gold Pennant|url=https://www.mirror.co.uk/sport/football/transfer-news/jermaine-pennant-joins-wolves-on-loan-1374561|work=Daily Mirror|date=12 October 2012|access-date=5 April 2018|archive-date=15 April 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180415063717/https://www.mirror.co.uk/sport/football/transfer-news/jermaine-pennant-joins-wolves-on-loan-1374561|url-status=live}}</ref>

[[File:Coat of arms of Wolverhampton.svg|thumb|left|City coat of arms.]]

Like most English teams, their earliest shirts usually only featured a badge on special occasions such as cup finals.<ref name="HistoricalKits"/> The first such badge to be worn on Wolves shirts was the coat of arms of the [[Wolverhampton City Council|County Borough of Wolverhampton]].<ref name="HistoricalKits"/> In the late 1960s, Wolves introduced their own club badge that appeared on their shirts consisting of a single leaping wolf, which later became three leaping wolves in the mid-1970s. Since 1979 the badge has consisted of a single "wolf head" design; the current badge was last redesigned in 2002.<ref name="HistoricalKits"/><ref name="BadgeLegalCase">{{cite news |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/uk-england-birmingham-48220428 |title=Wolves club badge design court battle begins |work=BBC News |date=9 May 2019 |access-date=2 June 2019 |archive-date=16 June 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190616023540/https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/uk-england-birmingham-48220428 |url-status=live }}</ref>

In May 2019, the club won a legal challenge by Peter Davies, a 71 year old retired building industry manager, who claimed he drew the wolf head motif as a schoolboy in the 1960s and entered it in an art competition. Mr Davies said he came up with the angular design after a teacher asked him to demonstrate an understanding of [[Blaise Pascal]]'s Hexagrammum Mysticum Theorem, and entered it in an art competition advertised in the Express and Star newspaper. Mr Davies had made a copyright claim and wanted compensation. Mr Davies lost his copyright infringement claim and now faces legal fees and costs estimated to be about £450,000.<ref>{{cite news |title=Wolverhampton Wanderers badge copyright claim thrown out |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/uk-england-birmingham-48288244 |access-date=8 September 2019 |agency=BBC |date=15 May 2019 |archive-date=24 October 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191024230456/https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/uk-england-birmingham-48288244 |url-status=live }}</ref>

Wolves' traditional away colours have been all-white, but recent decades have seen a variety of colours used, including black, blue, teal, purple and maroon.<ref name="HistoricalKits"/>

==Stadium==

===Former grounds===
When first founded the club used a field on Goldthorn Hill in the [[Blakenhall]] area as its home, which could accommodate some 2,000 spectators.<ref name="Matthews"/> In 1879 they relocated to John Harper's Field on Lower Villiers Street where they remained for two years before a short move to [[Dudley Road]], with the new ground situated opposite the Fighting Cocks Inn.<ref name="Matthews"/> It was here that they played their first [[FA Cup]] tie in 1883 and their first Football League fixture in September 1888. Although the site could only hold 2,500 spectators at first it was eventually developed to be capable of 10,000.<ref name="Matthews"/>

In the summer of 1889 the club moved to its permanent home ever since, [[Molineux Stadium|Molineux]], in the [[Whitmore Reans]] area of the city. The stadium name originates from the [[Molineux Hotel|Molineux House]] built in the area by Benjamin Molineux, a local merchant, in the 18th century and whose grounds were later developed to include numerous public leisure facilities. When the Northampton Brewery Company purchased these grounds in 1889, they rented their use to the city's football club, who were seeking to find a home more befitting a Football League member.<ref name="Matthews"/> After renovating the site, the first ever official game was staged on 7 September 1889 before a crowd of 4,000.<ref name="Matthews"/> The ground was capable of hosting 20,000 spectators, although English football crowds rarely reached that number in the 19th century.<ref name="Matthews"/>

Wolves bought the [[freehold (law)|freehold]] in 1923 and soon began a series of ground improvements under the auspices of [[Archibald Leitch]],<ref>{{cite web|url=http://molineuxstadiumthroughtheages.blogspot.com/p/molineux-archibald-leitch.html|title=Molineux - Archibald Leitch|publisher=molineuxstadiumthroughtheages.blogspot.com|access-date=7 October 2018|archive-date=8 October 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181008061246/http://molineuxstadiumthroughtheages.blogspot.com/p/molineux-archibald-leitch.html|url-status=live}}</ref> beginning with the construction of a major grandstand on the Waterloo Road side.<ref name="Programme">{{cite book |title=100 Years of Molineux 1889–1989: Special Souvenir Programme |year=1989 |publisher=Wolverhampton Wanderers F.C}}</ref> In 1932, the club also built a new stand on the Molineux Street side and followed this by adding a roof to the South Bank two years later; this South Bank was historically the second largest of all [[Spion Kop (stadiums)|Kop ends]] in the country and regularly held crowds in excess of 30,000.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.expressandstar.com/sport/wolverhampton-wanderers-fc/2011/02/10/launch-of-a-golden-vision-at-molineux/|title=Launch of a golden vision at Molineux|publisher=Express & Star|date=10 February 2011|access-date=21 March 2018|archive-date=27 February 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170227100646/http://www.expressandstar.com/sport/wolverhampton-wanderers-fc/2011/02/10/launch-of-a-golden-vision-at-molineux/|url-status=live}}</ref> The stadium finally now had four complete stands that would form its basis for the next half-century.

In the days before seating regulations, the ground could hold more than 60,000 spectators, with the record attendance being 61,315 for a [[Football League First Division|First Division]] match against [[Liverpool F.C.|Liverpool]] on 11 February 1939.<ref name="Matthews"/> The 1940s and 1950s saw average attendances for seasons regularly exceed 40,000, coinciding with the club's peak on the field.<ref name="Matthews"/> During this time Molineux became one of the first British grounds to install floodlights, enabling it to host a series of midweek friendlies against teams from around the globe.<ref name="Programme"/> In the days prior to the formation of the [[UEFA Champions League|European Cup]] and international club competitions, these games were highly prestigious and gained huge crowds and interest, with the [[BBC]] often televising such events.<ref name="European"/><ref>{{cite news|title=Football from top to bottom|url=https://www.independent.co.uk/sport/football/news-and-comment/football-from-top-to-bottom-994699.html|work=The Independent|date=6 November 2008|access-date=5 December 2017|archive-date=15 April 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180415065027/https://www.independent.co.uk/sport/football/news-and-comment/football-from-top-to-bottom-994699.html|url-status=live}}</ref>

When the Molineux Street Stand failed to meet new safety legislation, the club began building a new replacement stand behind the existing one on land where housing had been demolished. This new all-seater stand – named the John Ireland Stand after the then-club president – was completed in 1979 and was the first stage of a plan to rebuild the entire stadium.<ref name="Programme"/> The cost of the Ireland Stand escalated to over £2 million and plunged the club into a financial crisis. As a result, it was forced to enter receivership in 1982.<ref name="Programme"/> By the time the team dropped into the [[Football League Fourth Division|Fourth Division]] in 1986, only the John Ireland Stand and the South Bank terrace remained in use. New safety laws were implemented following the [[Bradford City stadium fire]] and these forced the closure of both the now-dilapidated North Bank and Waterloo Road Stand. The club did not have the funds necessary to rebuild them.<ref name="Programme"/>

Following the takeover of the club by [[Jack Hayward|Sir Jack Hayward]] in 1990, £8.5 million of funding was made available to redevelop Molineux comprehensively.<ref name="Matthews"/> Between August 1991 and December 1993 three sides of the stadium were completely rebuilt to form a 28,525 capacity all-seater stadium that complied with the [[Taylor Report]]: the Waterloo Road Stand was replaced by the [[Billy Wright (footballer born 1924)|Billy Wright]] Stand, the North Bank terrace by the [[Stan Cullis]] Stand, and the South Bank terrace by the Sir Jack Hayward Stand (named the Jack Harris Stand until 2015).<ref name="Matthews"/> Aside from the addition of a temporary seating area in the southwest corner used during Wolves' seasons in the Premier League;<ref>{{cite web|title=Ground capacity raised|url=http://www.wolves.co.uk/page/News/0,,10307~390175,00.html|publisher=Wolverhampton Wanderers F.C|date=11 June 2003|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120902140854/http://www.wolves.co.uk/page/News/0,,10307~390175,00.html|archive-date=2 September 2012}}</ref> this redevelopment formed the stadium for almost twenty years.

In 2010, plans were unveiled for an extensive redevelopment programme to enlarge the capacity and develop the facilities.<ref name="Plans">{{cite web|title=Wolves unveil Molineux redevelopment plans|url=http://www.wolves.co.uk/page/News/0,,10307~2060349,00.html|publisher=Wolverhampton Wanderers F.C |date=28 May 2010|url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120630054439/http://www.wolves.co.uk/page/News/0,,10307~2060349,00.html |archive-date=30 June 2012}}</ref> The first stage of this saw a new two-tier Stan Cullis Stand become fully operational for [[2012–13 Wolverhampton Wanderers F.C. season|the 2012–13 season]], raising the current official capacity to 31,700.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.wolves.co.uk/news/article/stan-cullis-stand-official-opening-090812-302651.aspx?pageView=full|title=Stan Cullis Stand official opening|publisher=Wolverhampton Wanderers F.C|date=24 August 2012|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170605023047/http://www.wolves.co.uk/news/article/stan-cullis-stand-official-opening-090812-302651.aspx?pageView=full|archive-date=5 June 2017}}</ref> The proposed second stage concerned the rebuilding of the oldest stand at the stadium (built in 1979 as the John Ireland Stand and renamed the Steve Bull Stand in 2003) to increase capacity to around 36,000, but this and any further work was shelved when it became likely that the club would be relegated from the Premier League in 2012.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.wolves.co.uk/page/News/0,,10307~2581694,00.html |title=Wolves to postpone Steve Bull Stand redevelopment |publisher=Wolverhampton Wanderers F.C |date=19 January 2012 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120122075352/http://www.wolves.co.uk/page/News/0,,10307~2581694,00.html |archive-date=22 January 2012}}</ref>

Ground redevelopments were once again placed on the agenda following the club's acquisition by Fosun in 2016. In contrast to previously mooted plans,<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.expressandstar.com/sport/football/wolverhampton-wanderers-fc/2018/03/03/revealed-wolves-plan-for-huge-south-bank/|title=Revealed: ===Managerial history===
[[File:StanCullisStatue.jpg|thumb|Statue of Stan Cullis outside Molineux.]]
{{Main|List of Wolverhampton Wanderers F.C. managers}}

Wolves have had 32 different (permanently appointed) managers during the club's existence.<ref name="Managers">{{cite news|title=Wolves: Manager history|url=http://www.soccerbase.com/teams/team.sd?team_id=2848&teamTabs=managers|publisher=Soccerbase|access-date=4 April 2013|archive-date=7 November 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121107191341/http://www.soccerbase.com/teams/team.sd?team_id=2848&teamTabs=managers|url-status=live}}</ref> The first manager, [[George Worrall]], was identified by the title of "club secretary", a post that continued until the appointment of a full-time manager in the modern sense was made in 1922.

The club's most successful manager is [[Stan Cullis]], whose 16-year tenure brought all three of Wolves' league championships as well as two FA Cup triumphs.<ref>{{cite news |title=Stan Cullis |url=http://www.wolves.co.uk/news/article/hof-stan-cullis-2009-421286.aspx?pageView=full |publisher=Wolverhampton Wanderers F.C |date=16 January 2009 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131224111032/http://www.wolves.co.uk/news/article/hof-stan-cullis-2009-421286.aspx?pageView=full|archive-date=24 December 2013 }}</ref> Two other managers have been inducted into the Club Hall of Fame: [[Frank Buckley (footballer)|Major Frank Buckley]] and [[Graham Turner]].<ref>{{cite news |title=Hall of Fame Inductee Announcement |url=http://www.wolves.co.uk/news/article/hall-of-fame-buckley-and-honved-261012-448288.aspx?pageView=full |publisher=Wolverhampton Wanderers F.C. |date=26 October 2012 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131224111746/http://www.wolves.co.uk/news/article/hall-of-fame-buckley-and-honved-261012-448288.aspx?pageView=full |archive-date=24 December 2013 }}</ref><ref>{{cite news |title=Graham Turner |url=http://www.wolves.co.uk/news/article/hof-graham-turner-2010-421632.aspx?pageView=full |publisher=Wolverhampton Wanderers F.C. |date=14 January 2010 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151123041925/http://www.wolves.co.uk/news/article/hof-graham-turner-2010-421632.aspx?pageView=full |archive-date=23 November 2015 }}</ref> Turner oversaw two successive divisional championship wins in the late-1980s, winning the [[1987-88 Football League#Fourth Division|Fourth Division title in 1987-88]] and the [[1988-89 Football League#Third Division|Third Division title the following season]]. [[Bill McGarry (footballer)|Bill McGarry]] and [[John Barnwell]] both won the [[League Cup]] for Wolves in the 1970s and 1980s.<ref name="Managers"/>

In the 21st century, [[Dave Jones (footballer, born 1956)|Dave Jones]], [[Mick McCarthy]] and [[Nuno Espírito Santo]] have led the club into the [[Premier League]]. [[Kenny Jackett]] took Wolves to a record [[EFL League One]] (Tier 3) points haul of 103 as they won this division in [[2013–14 Football League One|2013–14]].

[[Ståle Solbakken]] became Wolves' first foreign manager under [[Steve Morgan (businessman)|Steve Morgan]]'s ownership, followed later by [[Walter Zenga]], two Portuguese managers [[Nuno Espírito Santo]] and [[Bruno Lage]], and [[Julen Lopetegui]] who is Spanish, under current owners [[Fosun]].

Wolves have also been managed by two former [[England national football team|England national team]] managers in [[Graham Taylor]] and [[Glenn Hoddle]].<ref name="Managers"/>

===Rivalries===
{{See also|Wolverhampton Wanderers F.C. league record by opponent}}
Wolves' longest-established and strongest rivalry is with [[West Bromwich Albion F.C.|West Bromwich Albion]], against whom the club contest the [[Black Country derby]]. The two clubs, separated by eleven miles, have faced each other 163 times;<ref name="Derby stats">{{cite web| title=Head to head: Wolverhampton Wanderers vs. West Bromwich Albion| url=https://www.soccerbase.com/teams/head_to_head.sd?team_id=2848&team2_id=2744| publisher=Soccerbase| access-date=9 February 2024| archive-date=11 September 2018| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180911050248/http://www.soccerbase.com/teams/head_to_head.sd?team_id=2848&team2_id=2744| url-status=live}}</ref> with the Baggies winning 65, Wolves winning 54 and 44 ending in a draw. Their first competitive clash being an [[FA Cup]] tie in 1886.<ref name="Derby stats"/> A national survey by the [[football pools]] found the rivalry to be the strongest in English football.<ref name="Rivalries League">{{cite web| title=Rivalries League| url=http://www.footballpools.com/football-fever/Rivalries_Report_2008.pdf| publisher=The New Football Pools| date=February 2008| url-status=dead| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131015233159/http://www.footballpools.com/football-fever/Rivalries_Report_2008.pdf| archive-date=15 October 2013| df=dmy-all}}</ref> Both clubs are founder members of the Football League and the two once contested the league title in [[1953–54 Wolverhampton Wanderers F.C. season|1953–54]], with Wolves finishing as champions.<ref>{{cite web| title=When the Black Country rivals Wolves and West Bromwich Albion ruled English football| url=http://www.birminghammail.co.uk/sport/football/football-news/when-the-black-country-rivals-wolves-and-west-178706| publisher=Birmingham Mail| date=9 February 2012| access-date=7 February 2013| archive-date=16 October 2013| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131016033055/http://www.birminghammail.co.uk/sport/football/football-news/when-the-black-country-rivals-wolves-and-west-178706| url-status=live}}</ref>

Wolves also share rivalries with the two Birmingham clubs, [[Aston Villa F.C.|Aston Villa]] and [[Birmingham City F.C.|Birmingham City]], against whom there have been numerous matches dating back to the 19th century.<ref>{{cite web |title=Head to head: Wolves v Aston Villa |url=http://www.soccerbase.com/teams/head_to_head.sd?team_id=2848&team2_id=154 |publisher=Soccerbase |access-date=7 February 2013 |archive-date=24 December 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131224120616/http://www.soccerbase.com/teams/head_to_head.sd?team_id=2848&team2_id=154 |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Head to head: Wolves v Birmingham City |url=http://www.soccerbase.com/teams/head_to_head.sd?team_id=2848&team2_id=291 |publisher=Soccerbase |access-date=7 February 2013 |archive-date=24 December 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131224115739/http://www.soccerbase.com/teams/head_to_head.sd?team_id=2848&team2_id=291 |url-status=live }}</ref> Wolves' closest geographic rival is actually [[Walsall F.C.|Walsall]] but, as they have rarely competed at the same level,<ref>{{cite web |title=Head to head: Wolves v Walsall |url=http://www.soccerbase.com/teams/head_to_head.sd?team_id=2848&team2_id=2737 |publisher=Soccerbase |access-date=7 February 2013 |archive-date=4 June 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160604151758/http://www.soccerbase.com/teams/head_to_head.sd?team_id=2848&team2_id=2737 |url-status=live }}</ref> it is of less significance. As Wolverhampton historically sat within the boundaries of [[Staffordshire]], a Staffordshire derby between Wolves and [[Stoke City F.C.|Stoke City]] is also recognised.

The 2018–19 Premier League season was the first and only time ever that Wolves were the sole representatives of the West Midlands in the top flight of English football. The 2020–21 Premier League season saw Wolves play against both Aston Villa and West Bromwich Albion.<ref name="Rivalries resumed">{{cite web| title=Rivalries renewed as long-awaited derbies return| url=https://www.premierleague.com/news/1755940| publisher=Premier League| date=21 August 2020| access-date=15 October 2020| archive-date=25 October 2020| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201025202806/https://www.premierleague.com/news/1755940| url-status=live}}</ref> Since Albion's relegation at the end of that season, Aston Villa has been Wolves' only West Midlands rival in the Premier League.

===Fan culture===
During the club's peak in the 1950s, the home crowd's signature song was "[[The Happy Wanderer]]", which was a chart hit in the U.K. in 1954 when Wolves first won the league title.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.officialcharts.com/charts/singles-chart/19540319/7501/ | title=Official Singles Chart Top 12: 19–25 March 1954 | publisher=The Official UK Charts Company | date=30 April 2019 | access-date=30 April 2019 | archive-date=30 April 2019 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190430032343/https://www.officialcharts.com/charts/singles-chart/19540319/7501/ | url-status=live }}</ref> In more recent times, "[[Hi Ho Silver Lining]]" – a 1967 rock song by [[Jeff Beck]] with its chorus modified to ''"Hi Ho Wolverhampton!"'' – has become a staple feature of home games.<ref>{{cite web| title=The Football Ground Guide: Molineux |url=http://www.footballgroundguide.com/wolverhampton_wanderers/index.htm#Visiting-Molineux | publisher=The Football Ground Guide| url-status=dead| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130217130801/http://www.footballgroundguide.com/wolverhampton_wanderers/index.htm#Visiting-Molineux| archive-date=17 February 2013| df=dmy-all}}</ref> "[[The Liquidator (instrumental)|The Liquidator]]" instrumental by the [[Harry J. Allstars]] was also popularly used in the stadium until a request from the [[West Midlands Police]] to cease due to concerns that the obscene lyrics used by some fans during the chorus could incite trouble.<ref>{{cite news| title=Can we play you every week?| url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/sport2/hi/funny_old_game/1680656.stm| publisher=[[BBC Sport]]| date=28 November 2001| access-date=28 September 2007| archive-date=13 January 2016| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160113022820/http://news.bbc.co.uk/sport1/hi/funny_old_game/1680656.stm| url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web| title=Wolverhampton Council (Licensing and Environmental Protection Panel) Meeting| url=http://www.wolverhampton.gov.uk/NR/rdonlyres/15397180-2094-4B5E-871B-CC4725E39132/0/limi210503.pdf| publisher=Wolverhampton Council| date=21 May 2003| url-status=dead| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080227065704/http://www.wolverhampton.gov.uk/NR/rdonlyres/15397180-2094-4B5E-871B-CC4725E39132/0/limi210503.pdf| archive-date=27 February 2008| df=dmy-all}}</ref>

The club attracted a number of hooligans in the 1960s. During the late 1970s and early 1980s, a [[hooligan firm]] named "The Subway Army" would often ambush fans in the [[Subway (underpass)|subway]] adjacent to the ground. The group was gradually broken up and virtually ceased to exist due to a large number of arrests – many as part of the police's nationwide "Operation GROWTH" (or "Get Rid of Wolverhampton's Troublesome Hooligans") in the late 1980s.<ref>{{cite book | author=Gary Armstrong and Dick Hobbs | editor = Richard Giulianotti, Norman Bonney and Mike Hepworth | title = Football, Violence and Social Identity | year = 1994 | publisher=Routledge | location = London | isbn = 0-415-09838-6 | pages = 196–228 | chapter = Tackled from behind}}</ref>

The club invites interaction with its supporters and has a Fans' Parliament, at which independently selected candidates meet with club officials discuss issues relating to the club.<ref>{{cite web| title=Fans' Parliament| url=https://www.wolves.co.uk/fans/fans-parliament/| publisher=Wolverhampton Wanderers F.C| access-date=25 September 2020| archive-date=20 October 2020| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201020210105/https://www.wolves.co.uk/fans/fans-parliament/| url-status=live}}</ref> An independent [[fanzine]] named ''A Load of Bull'' (ALOB), in part a reference to leading goalscorer [[Steve Bull]], published supporters' views between 1989 and 2012.<ref>{{cite news| title=Fanzine Focus – A Load of Bull 1989–2012| url =http://www.junkarchive.co.uk/wordpress/| publisher =Junk Archive blog| date =30 March 2012| url-status=dead| archive-url =https://web.archive.org/web/20120420014534/http://www.junkarchive.co.uk/wordpress/| archive-date =20 April 2012| df =dmy-all}}</ref><ref>{{cite news| title = A Load of Bull: End of an era| url = http://www.wolves.co.uk/page/News/0,,10307~2705979,00.html| publisher = Wolverhampton Wanderers F.C| date = 30 March 2012| url-status=dead| archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20120405174851/http://www.wolves.co.uk/page/News/0,,10307~2705979,00.html| archive-date = 5 April 2012| df = dmy-all}}</ref>

The club is owned by the Chinese conglomerate group [[Fosun International]], which purchased the parent company of the club, W.W. ==League history==
{{See also|List of Wolverhampton Wanderers F.C. seasons}}
Wolverhampton Wanderers was a founder member of the Football League in 1888. The 2025–26 season is Wolves' 127th in the Football League system. Wolves have spent 120 of their 126 completed seasons to date within the top two tiers of English football. Wolves played in the third tier on four occasions, each occasion lasting just one season; three of these seasons ended with promotion back to the second tier as Champions, and one ended in relegation to the fourth tier. The club has played two seasons in England's fourth tier (in the 1980s).
